Question: Was ancient Greek mythology influenced by ancient Egypt and Iran?
Answer: By all means. Truth be told, all the cultures that originated (or neighbored) the Fertile Crescent had common myths and deities, most myths have their roots in Mesopotamia. Obviously, these very ancient stories traveled westward along with the Anatolian farmers as they moved increasingly westward toward Europe or via trade roots. The Greeks (the Mycenaeans also before them), being merchants, traveled a lot and brought back home not only goods from foreign lands but also their stories. expansion of farming in W. Eurasia. Image credit Expansion of farming in western Eurasia, 9600 - 4000 cal BC (update vers. 2021.2) The difference with the Greeks is that their adaptations are impeccable. They tailored the Mesopotamian stories and deities to their own measures, removing any element that didn't fit them so well that for some, we wouldn't understand their origin if we didn't find the originals. For example, the song of Koumarbi. Hesiod’s Theogony is practically the Greek version of the Hittite song of Kumarbi (see the details in the link in the footnotes). The story is not a Hittite one either but a Hurrian one (the Hurrians lived throughout northern Syria, upper Mesopotamia, and southeastern Anatolia). And how about the similarity between Zeus and the Egyptian Amun? Herodotus states: Then, holding the head before him and covering himself in the fleece, he showed himself to Heracles. This story explains why the Egyptians represent Zeus with a ram's head—a practice, which has extended to the Ammonians, who are a joint colony of Egyptians and Ethiopians ... So far as I can see, the Ammonians took their name too from the circumstance; for Amun is the Egyptian name for Zeus.” It is impossible to live in this region of the world without being influenced by the neighbors (or influencing them). Personally, I find the exchange of ideas a good thing, progress is its offspring… The Melammu Project (about the similarities between Theogony and the song of Kumarbi) Oriental Forerunners of Hesiod on JSTOR

Question: What was bathing like in Ancient Rome or Greece?
Answer: Personal hygiene was a serious matter for both Greeks and Romans (I can say they were bathing freaks…) and cleansing themselves was more than a ritual. They might bathe at home, in their bathtub, in their bathroom. This is an image from ancient Olynthos (it was destroyed and abandoned in 318 BCE). The children look at an ancient bath. The bath might be a clay-made seated bath (like in the image above) or a basin made of clay or marble (like below). Three young women bathing. Side B from an Attic red-figure stamnos, 440/30 BC. Accession number Inv. 2411, Staatliche Antikensammlungen, Munich, Germany Treatments with aromatic oils and beauty products for women would follow (a manicure and pedicure were necessary). image from Pinterest A shower was an option too image from Hellenica World Hot water or cold water? That depends on who you ask. The Spartans and the Macedonians preferred the cold ones as they believed that hot baths caused softness. The Athenians on the other hand, used hot and cold baths, which they considered a factor of health and culture. What about soap? The Greeks didn’t use soap. However, they had an effective cleansing method. They rub their body with ash and oils (the potassium of the ash and the oil make a natural soap) and then scrub it with pumice. Using a strigil (stleggis in Greek) they removed the remains of oil and ash and then doused them with water. Finally, they rub down with oil. a strigil of the classic period http://MetMuseum.com They could also take their bath in public facilities, the valaneia. The oldest ones we know of operated in Sybaris, an ancient city of Magna Graecia in southern Italy, at the end of the 6th century BCE. The valaneia appeared in Athens in the 5th century BCE, but their spread continued to be great during the Hellenistic period. The public baths could be of public or private ownership and were usually built close to gymnasiums. Athletes' baths in Nemea Bathing was also an important part of medical treatment. Hippocrates was the first to systematically study the therapeutic use of hot and cold baths and dissociate it from religion. He classified the waters into three categories: drinking water, salty water, and seawater. By "salty water" he meant thermal waters. The Romans continued and improved the use of public baths. The Roman public baths (the thermae) were used both for personal hygiene and socialization. They could be truly luxurious! Thermae from the city of Herculaneum A Roman would go first to the calidarium (warm pool), before moving on to the tepidarium (lukewarm pool) and frigidarium (cold pool). Finally, they will swim in the natatium, which is an outdoor pool. To ensure the hygiene of the facility, the architects of the baths planned the flow of water through and through the hot and cold basins. The necessary thousands of cubic meters of water were provided by aqueducts. Water will flow into a large tank in the main building where a distribution system either brings water to the cold pools or over wood burning for the use of hot and hot baths. In terms of drainage, the floor of each room led to the drains that ran down the distribution pipes to direct water to the municipal drainage system. A hypocaust from Cyprus (where a log fire heated elevated marble floors, channeling hot air through pipes in the wall, raised the temperature to over 210 degrees F. Bathers had to wear special shoes to protect their feet). If we think of it, a few things are added today…right? Question: How did some ancient cities disappear? E.g troy, it was a big city but then after the war it fell from history and got covered by dirt for us to dig it up. Why didn't anyone else use that location to build again? (expanded question below)
Answer: Believe it or not, only nature can make a city disappear. Avalanches (like what happened to Aiges), submersions (like Pavlopetri), lava flow (Pompeii) are the reasons for a city to vanish. Destruction by human activity — war, or riots— or even earthquakes can result in temporary abandonment, and then life returns and the damaged cities are rebuilt. Pavlopetri was a Mycenaean city and port that submerged for natural causes ~1,000 BCE. Underwater city Pavlopetri – Laconia. Why? A settlement is created for a reason, it’s a port or the residence of the ruler or it’s simply close to a water source, and people don’t abandon them easily. Look what happened to Corinth, for instance; the Romans razed the city in 146 BCE but rebuilt it a hundred years later as it is a strategic spot. The same happened to Troy; the first settlement was founded ~3,600 BCE and turned into a city ~3,000 BCE. Nine times the city was destroyed by invasions and earthquakes and rebuilt afterward until it was finally abandoned in 500 CE after a strong earthquake. The earthquake was not the real reason for the abandonment. Troy lived for millennia because of its strategic location, it controlled the trade routes between the Aegean and the Black Sea. At the time of the final disaster, other ports (mainly Constantinople) had replaced its significance. The probable location of the ancient city of Troy. Provided by Graham Bartholomew/BBC/Wild Mercury Productions Even when a city is eventually abandoned (because some other location has replaced its importance or its resources have run out) it takes centuries if not millennia to be buried. Take Mycenae for instance, the Bronze Age citadel was never buried. A gravure by E. Breton (1846), decades before Schliemann’s excavation. Porte Des Lions a Mycenes

Question: How prominent is Greek mythology in modern Greek culture? Is it referenced often in idioms, quotes, politics, social media, news, etc?
Answer: It is, with the Homeric epics having the largest share. We often use phrases like: "Achilles' heel" to describe the vulnerable point of a person or a plan. "Trojan horse" to describe a plan that appears beneficial while hiding unpleasant aspects. A good equivalent is the cheese in the trap. “Iphigenia” is someone who pretends they make a personal sacrifice falsely; “don’t pretend Iphigenia to me”. We go “from Scylla to Charybdis” every time we move from a bad situation to a worse one. A beautiful woman is often described as “Helen of Troy”. We even use genuine phrases from the epics like “’επεα πτερόεντα” (flying words) to describe a speech or saying that has no real value or will be forgotten soon. From other myths: A “Labyrinth” is any building (or situation) that is intricate. “I open Pandora’s box” each time I create a sequence of harmful situations.
